variants.hook: Most engineers think code review is about catching bugs. It isn't.
variants.body:
Most engineers think code review is about catching bugs. It isn't.

When I led backend at Acme Corp, our best reviews caught almost no bugs -- they caught knowledge gaps. A junior engineer's PR taught three seniors something about our own system.

That's the real value: a shared understanding of the codebase, built one review at a time.
variants.cta: What's the best thing a code review has taught you?
variants.hook_rationale: Opens with a common assumption, then contradicts it -- creates curiosity.

variants.hook: I used to dread code review. Now I look forward to it.
variants.body:
I used to dread code review. Now I look forward to it.

The shift happened when I stopped treating it as a gate and started treating it as a conversation. At Acme Corp, that meant leaving questions instead of directives: "what happens if this input is empty?" instead of "handle the empty case."

Same outcome, completely different feeling on both sides.
variants.cta: Try asking one question in your next review instead of giving one directive.
variants.hook_rationale: A personal before/after creates a relatable arc readers want resolved.

variants.hook: Three years leading backend teams taught me this about feedback:
variants.body:
Three years leading backend teams taught me this about feedback: the delivery matters more than the content.

The exact same suggestion, phrased as a question versus a command, gets adopted at wildly different rates. I saw this firsthand managing distributed systems reviews at Acme Corp.

It's not about being soft. It's about staying curious.
variants.hook_rationale: Numbered credibility ("three years") signals experience before the payoff.
